title: In Meghalaya, Living Root Bridges Grow Stronger With Every Passing Year
excerpt: Khasi and Jaintia villagers guide the roots of rubber fig trees across rivers for decades, creating self-healing bridges now nominated for UNESCO World Heritage status.
body:
• Meghalaya's living root bridges, grown from the aerial roots of rubber fig trees by the Khasi and Jaintia tribes over 15 to 30 years, are India's latest nomination for UNESCO World Heritage status.
  • Unlike conventional bridges that deteriorate with age, these structures strengthen over time and can support 50 people at once, with lifespans stretching to 500 years.
  • Researchers have documented at least 75 living root bridges in the region, with the famous double-decker bridge at Nongriat village estimated to be around 200 years old.

Bridges That Grow Stronger With Age

In the mist-covered hills of Meghalaya, India's northeastern state that receives among the highest rainfall on Earth, the Khasi and Jaintia peoples have spent centuries solving an engineering problem with patience rather than concrete. Their solution: living bridges grown from the aerial roots of the Indian rubber fig tree, Ficus elastica, trained across rivers and gorges over decades until they form load-bearing structures that get stronger with every passing year.

The bridges, known locally as Jingkieng Jri, are formed by guiding young, pliable roots along bamboo scaffolds or hollowed-out betel nut trunks stretched across waterways. Over 15 to 30 years, the roots thicken, intertwine, and fuse through a natural process called inosculation, creating a self-reinforcing lattice strong enough to hold 50 or more people at a time, according to research documented by National Geographic and the Smithsonian.

A UNESCO Bid for Global Recognition

India formally submitted Meghalaya's living root bridges for inclusion on UNESCO's World Heritage List for the 2026-27 cycle, with India's Ambassador to UNESCO Vishal V. Sharma handing over the nomination dossier to UNESCO Director Lazare Assomo Eloundou earlier this year.

"We are hopeful that the living root bridges will be inscribed this year, ensuring that the indigenous communities, the true guardians of this living heritage, receive the global recognition they so richly deserve."

— Conrad K. Sangma, Chief Minister of Meghalaya

The nomination recognizes not just the bridges as structures but the cultural landscape of indigenous knowledge that sustains them. Each bridge requires active, multigenerational care — pruning, guiding new shoots, clearing debris — making them as much a living tradition as a living structure.

Where Monsoon Engineering Meets Heritage

The bridges exist because conventional construction fails here. Meghalaya's Cherrapunji region receives roughly 12 meters (40 feet) of rainfall annually, turning streams into violent torrents that destroy wooden and steel bridges. The root bridges, anchored to living trees, flex rather than break, and repair themselves by growing new root material into damaged sections.

Researchers geo-located 75 living root bridges in a 2017 survey, most growing on steep subtropical slopes between 50 and 1,150 meters above sea level. The most famous is the double-decker bridge at Nongriat village — two parallel decks measuring approximately 80 and 60 feet, both extending from a single Indian rubber tree over the Mawsaw River. The second, higher deck was built after monsoon flooding made the lower crossing dangerous. The structure is estimated to be around 200 years old.

Tourism Boom and Its Tensions

The bridges have become a significant draw for domestic and international tourists. By 2023, annual tourist footfall in Meghalaya had doubled over the previous decade, according to a Smithsonian report. Nongriat, once an obscure village with a single community homestay, now has more than half a dozen lodging options. Many residents who once farmed now work as guides, leading visitors down roughly 3,500 steps into the valley.

But tourism has also introduced stress. The health of the Umshiang Double-Decker Root Bridge has degraded due to visitor traffic, according to Wikipedia. A replica has been constructed nearby to present the Khasi craft without further straining the original. Balancing access with preservation is among the challenges that the UNESCO nomination, if successful, would need to address.

Why the Bridges Still Matter

For the Khasi villagers, these structures are not tourist attractions but lifelines. During heavy monsoon months, when rivers can swell into impassable torrents within hours, a root bridge may be the only connection between a village and its schools, markets, and neighbors. Without them, communities would face weeks of isolation.

The bridges also represent a form of engineering that Western science is only beginning to study seriously. Researchers note that the combination of continuous growth and active human maintenance creates structures of such complexity that "simple mechanical analysis" is unfeasible, according to a study cited by the Smithsonian. In an era of climate adaptation, an infrastructure tradition that strengthens with time rather than decaying offers lessons that extend well beyond Meghalaya's hills.
image_caption: A living root bridge in Meghalaya formed from the aerial roots of rubber fig trees. These structures, maintained by the Khasi people for centuries, grow stronger with each passing year.
nri_angle: The living root bridges of Meghalaya represent a unique piece of Indian heritage now gaining global recognition, offering diaspora travelers a compelling reason to explore the northeast.
